transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks, spots, the sagging—I feel like every banker or county person I deal with is staring at it. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, but it doesn’t feel that way to me.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your face and hands in mirrors or other reflective surfaces?

Yes. Before a loan meeting or setting up at a craft fair, I’ll check the bathroom mirror, then the truck mirror again. I keep turning my hat, looking at my face and hands, comparing my hands to the younger workers’. Next thing I know I’ve burned time I ought to be using on the farm.
Do these distressing thoughts and checking behaviors happen even when you are alone at home with no plans to see anyone?

Mostly it’s before I have to go meet somebody. I’ll check the bathroom mirror, then the truck mirror, keep adjusting my hat and looking at my hands next to the younger workers’. It can eat up time I should be spending on the farm.
Aside from how your face and hands look, do you feel anxious about speaking, making a mistake, or embarrassing yourself when meeting people?
I’m not sure. I mostly just get caught up in how I look when I’m going to meet people.
Do you have any other repetitive habits or routines, like repeatedly checking doors or washing, that have nothing to do with your appearance?
No, I haven’t really noticed other routines like that. It’s mainly the appearance checking.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates persistent preoccupation with imagined or slight defects in physical appearance (rough, worn skin, spots, sagging on face and hands) that is out of proportion to reality, along with repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, comparing appearance, adjusting hat) causing noticeable distress and functional interference. In ICD-10, Body Dysmorphic Disorder is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder).

confirmed_symptoms: Preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance (rough/worn face and hands, cracks, spots, sagging)
Belief that others are staring at perceived physical defects
Repetitive mirror checking (bathroom and truck mirrors)
Repetitive comparison of physical appearance to others (hands next to younger workers)
Repetitive camouflaging/adjusting behaviors (turning and adjusting hat)

additional_requirements: Symptoms consume significant time and interfere with farm work responsibilities
Absence of broader non-appearance-related obsessive-compulsive rituals
